## Chapter 7: Creating the Right Environment for Data-Aware Design

This chapter outlines three principles for establishing an organizational environment where data-informed design can flourish: shared company culture and values, hiring the right people, and supportive processes. The chapter emphasizes that embedding data literacy throughout an organization requires deliberate cultural, structural, and procedural changes.

### Principle 1: Shared Company Culture and Values

**Depth: Communicating Across Levels**

Data literacy fundamentally reshapes decision-making hierarchies. A data-literate environment diminishes reliance on "gut" decisions and top-down hunches, replacing hierarchical authority with evidence-based discussion where anyone can challenge assumptions and potentially be wrong. Grounded user data—gathered through A/B testing, ethnographic research, field deployments, surveys, and usability studies—provides a less risky foundation than individual executive intuition.

A 2007 paper by Ron Kohavi, Randal Henne, and Dan Sommerfield, "Practical Guide to Controlled Experiments on the Web: Listen to Your Customers not to the HIPPO," established this principle: data resolves conflicts without relying on rank or company politics. John Ciancutti, former VP of Product Engineering at Netflix, described how data literacy across all roles became a source of freedom and innovation. Patty McCord, Netflix's Chief Talent Officer for over 12 years, noted that measuring whether you're doing the right thing for customers allows more people to have a voice in product development.

Netflix's data-driven approach was well established and universally accepted company-wide. While it may have started with CEO Reed Hastings and CPO Neil Hunt driving the practice, it was embraced throughout the organization from management to individual contributors. Patty McCord observed that at Netflix, unlike companies where the CEO might do whatever he wants, even executives can get caught up in thinking they know the answer. A/B testing mitigates this tendency because everyone can learn from experimentation.

Reed Hastings himself submitted his product ideas to the same A/B testing rigor as everyone else on the product team. On rare occasions when he dictated exactly how a product idea would work, he would do so on "his test cell"—an experimental group that was tested against other cells proposed by the product team. If it didn't win, it didn't launch. This accountability reinforced subjecting all ideas to grounded review through experimentation and treating "failure" as a positive outcome.

For organizations shifting toward data-aware frameworks, examining how product and design decisions have been made is critical. If decisions were largely concentrated among one or two individuals, those people must understand and recognize the value of incorporating user data—understanding that their weight in decisions will diminish along with the weight of any individual opinion.
